name: Suriname
summary_text: Suriname has not criminalised consensual same-sex conduct since 1869, and that position applies to men and women nationwide. Following the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the Penal Code was revised so that the age of consent is the same for same-sex and opposite-sex relations.  In March 2015 Articles 175, 175a and 176 of the Penal Code were revised to reach discrimination and hate speech grounded in sexual orientation. Whether those provisions extend to gender identity is not stated in the sources available here.  Protection otherwise rests on an implied reading rather than an express statute. Article 8.2 of the Constitution of Suriname lists 'any other status' among prohibited grounds, and the government treats that clause as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity. No statutory instrument enumerates sexual orientation or gender identity as protected grounds.  Legal gender recognition is not available. A trans visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with their presentation should expect document checks to be difficult rather than routine, and the sources available here do not describe how Surinamese border authorities handle such documents.  Formal protection has not produced safe conditions. A July 2024 civil-society report filed with the UN Human Rights Committee records that LGBTI people face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation despite constitutional protection, and the US State Department's 2015 human rights report documented discrimination against LGBTI persons and other minorities in Suriname.  Registration of LGBTI organisations is permitted. The Surinamese state told the Human Rights Committee in July 2024 that its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, with monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission in place; committee experts pressed the delegation on implementation of a regional court's judgment concerning transgender identity.

name: Turks and Caicos Islands
summary_text: The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code on single-sex services do not automatically extend to the Turks and Caicos Islands. Local law governs the territory, and United Kingdom measures reach it only by Order in Council.  Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2001, decriminalised through the United Kingdom-led reform programme across the Caribbean, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.  The Court of Appeal ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar. Reading "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, the court held that a refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees, while leaving the statutory definition of marriage untouched. The ruling secures residence recognition for same-sex partners of residents; it does not establish a right to marry locally.  Transgender status is handled operationally through United Kingdom document channels rather than through a published local statute. The United Kingdom HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the territory, operational guidance covering nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor holding a United Kingdom passport with a changed gender marker can therefore expect that document to be treated as valid here; the underlying local legal instrument, if any, is not documented in the available sources.  The social climate favours discretion over visibility. A resident account from May 2009 described virtually no public information about gay life in the territory, no visible social scene, and privacy as the everyday norm, attributing this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands and full-citizen Belongers are a demographic minority. A visitor should read that account as dated and impressionistic rather than as a finding on violence risk.

name: Togo
summary_text: Togo criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The provision is the Penal Code offence of "acts against nature committed with an individual of one's sex", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment and a fine (Human Dignity Trust).  The United States Department of State's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices states that the same law also prohibits "promotion of same-sex conduct", a clause understood to reach advocacy and gender identity expression, and records that the provision was enforced during the reporting period. Because the offence is drafted in terms of sexual acts rather than identity, a trans visitor's exposure is not self-evident from the code alone; the practical risk attaches to visibility, conduct and advocacy, and the sources do not delimit where the promotion clause ends.  Violence or threats of violence targeting LGBTTQI persons were listed among significant human-rights issues in Togo's 2023 human rights report, and the 2022 report carried the same finding. The 2011 report for Togo separately documented official and societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people alongside security-force torture and impunity, indicating a pattern recorded across more than a decade of external reporting.  A 2015 Washington Blade account of interviews conducted in March 2015 describes Lomé's police as "particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists", and recounts the author's return to the site of a 2008 attack on him in the capital. This is a direct on-the-ground assertion of tourist exposure to policing in Lomé rather than a general crime observation.  An alternative report submitted to the United Nations Human Rights Committee in June 2021 by AAEC Togo and Synergia describes an active civil-society channel: the Togolese association works on HIV within MSM-TG populations under the National Strategic Plan 2016-2020, documents LGBT rights violations across Togo and francophone West Africa, and provides legal and judicial support to victims.
